claims.text: The target eutectic high-entropy alloy contains interwoven phases with different oxidation tendencies and corrosion resistance.
One phase can form a protective but brittle oxide layer at elevated temperature.
Temperatures around 800–900 °C promote in-situ oxide formation.
The oxide forms preferentially on one phase of the eutectic microstructure.
The oxide is brittle, mechanically weak, or nonuniformly adherent across the constituent phases.
Mechanical wear repeatedly removes the oxide film.
Removal of the oxide exposes anodic regions at phase boundaries or interfaces.
Galvanic differences between phases cause the newly exposed interfaces to corrode rapidly.
Localized corrosion weakens the microstructure and increases its susceptibility to wear.
Repeated oxide removal, corrosion, and oxide reformation establish a positive feedback loop between wear and corrosion.
Combined wear-corrosion produces greater total degradation than either wear-only or corrosion-only exposure.
Combined degradation exceeds the additive sum of degradation measured in separate wear-only and corrosion-only tests.
Wear depth increases under combined wear-corrosion relative to the matched separate exposures.
Corrosion severity, including corrosion current density, increases under combined wear-corrosion relative to the matched separate exposures.
Oxygen and chloride are required under the proposed boundary conditions to support aggressive localized corrosion.
The applied wear must be sufficient to remove the oxide intermittently but insufficient to melt the surface completely.
Elevated-temperature wear behavior of an HEA changes substantially at 800–900 °C.

contradictions.description: The baseline calls for a wear-only specimen in the same corrosive atmosphere, while the intervention defines simultaneous abrasion and corrosive exposure as the combined condition. Unless the wear-only environment is made noncorrosive or corrosion is otherwise suppressed, that arm is not genuinely wear-only.
